sentences.text: Infernogallus is a small caenagnathid theropod estimated to weigh about 12 kg.
The holotype measures a femur length of 18.5 cm and suggests a mass between 9 and 15 kg.
Its skull preserves a large, circular orbit that occupies almost 40 % of the skull length.
Behind the eye, the infratemporal fenestra is very reduced, only about a quarter of the orbit’s diameter.
The left and right lower jaws are fused and curve steeply upward when seen laterally.
A long neck is built from twelve cervical vertebrae plus the atlas and axis, and the vertebrae are hollow with extensive air spaces.
The hands are elongated and capable of grasping.
The known material includes a partially articulated skull and skeleton together with several isolated cranial pieces.
The jaw muscles appear reorganized in a way that may have helped it eat fruit, a feature not seen in other non-avian theropods.
No gastroliths—stones used by some dinosaurs to grind food—were found with the fossils.
Infernogallus jamesi was formally named in October 2026 by Gregory F. Funston and colleagues.
The type locality lies within the Hell Creek Formation of the United States.
Fossils have been recovered from several sites in Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota, totaling five specimens.
Growth-ring analysis of the bones shows an external fundamental system, indicating the animal had reached skeletal maturity.
Histology suggests the individual was at least six, probably seven years old at death, having completed its growth.
The jaw structure allowed anteroposterior movement and featured ridged surfaces for crushing and shearing soft foods.
Enlarged palate muscles combined with reduced temporal muscles imply a weaker bite force compared with other oviraptorosaurs.
These features point to a specialized herbivorous diet focused on fleshy angiosperm fruits.
The animal likely defleshed fruit in a manner similar to modern parrots.
Infernogallus belongs to the family Caenagnathidae within the oviraptorosaurian theropods.
It is placed in the genus Infernogallus, with the sole species Infernogallus jamesi.
Phylogenetic analyses recover it among derived caenagnathids, grouped with taxa such as Anzu, Caenagnathus and Chirostenotes in a clade sometimes called Eucaenagnathinae.
It lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous, shortly after the appearance of fleshy angiosperm drupes.
Scientists disagree whether the jaw-muscle reorganization truly reflects an adaptation for fruit consumption.
The role of caenagnathids like Infernogallus in the Late Cretaceous spread of fruit remains uncertain.
Researchers caution against formally naming subclades such as “elmisaurins” because of instability in their relationships, even though some groupings appear consistent.
